topics: Results review: continuous batching impact on tokens/sec and latency
KV cache hit-rate and effect on effective throughput
Next tests: 24h stress run, canary configs
header: Date: 2027-07-14 | Start: 10:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Samir Patel, Lena Park, Diego Ramos (Redwood); Maya Chen, Omar Khalid, Priya Singh, Ethan Brooks (NovaPay)
transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, good morning, thanks for joining. We'll run about 45 minutes. quick agenda - results, tuning, next steps.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Morning, yep. we saw the earlier numbers you sent, um, a couple points we want to clarify on p95 numbers.
[00:33] Lena Park: cool. so to start, we re-ran continuous batching with the updated kernel selection patch, and overall tokens per second went up ~18% on avg, p95 dropped from about 320ms to ~240ms in the mid-load window. but under bursts we still see spikes.
[01:05] Omar Khalid: when you say bursts, do you mean short-lived RPS spikes, like a 10x burst for 30s? because our real traffic has those patterns.
[01:14] Lena Park: yeah exactly. when concurrency hits the cap and we start queueing, latencies can jump — p99 especially. we observed p99 at 1.2s in worst cases during synthetic bursts.
[01:33] Priya Singh: is that with KV cache warm? we suspected a cold cache would explain spikes.
[01:39] Diego Ramos: good call. these runs had the KV cache partially warmed; hit-rate around 65%. We expect more stable p95/p99 once hit-rate is >85% after steady-state.
[01:56] Ethan Brooks: and what's the concurrency setting in the run you shared? was it 32?
[02:03] Lena Park: that run was with concurrency target 32, continuous batching enabled, batch size cap at 64 tokens per micro-batch. we also tried 64 for comparison.
[02:15] Maya Chen: ok, show us the 64 numbers.
[02:18] Samir Patel: I pulled a quick summary into the sheet, link in chat — bit.ly/novapay-bench (note: internal). 64 gave higher throughput but slightly worse p95 under bursts due to queueing. average throughput improved ~25% vs 32, but p95 degraded from 240ms to 280ms under the same burst profile.
[02:45] Omar Khalid: so there's a trade-off — more concurrency = more throughput, but queue depth grows and latency tails worsen. what's Redwood recommendation here?
[02:55] Lena Park: for NovaPay's SLAs (p95 <= 220-250ms target), we'd recommend a hybrid: target concurrency 48 with dynamic scaling and a bounded queue of 500 requests, plus a hard cap that triggers fallback to a smaller, cheaper model for non-critical requests. this preserves tail latency while keeping throughput good.
[03:25] Priya Singh: fallback to smaller model — will that break outputs or change quality substantially?
[03:31] Lena Park: depends on prompt sensitivity. in our evals we saw minimal regression for templated flows — less than 3% decrease in accuracy for the scoring tasks you shared. for open prompts we recommend tagging requests so we don't route them to fallback.
[03:48] Maya Chen: hmm, tagging seems doable. our risk is the audit trail - we need clear logs showing which model served which request for compliance.
[03:56] Samir Patel: Redwood Console provides per-request model attribution and trace IDs. we can include those in the logs you ingest to Splunk — we've appended an example in the drive.
[04:10] Ethan Brooks: can we talk about queueing behavior? specifically fallback when queue full — does Redwood drop, reject, or queue externally?
[04:21] Diego Ramos: good question — by default our runtime will apply backpressure: once queue hits the configured limit, we either reject with a 429 or route to a fallback model/policy if configured. there's also an optional external queue integration for guaranteed burst smoothing (SQS/Kafka).
[04:40] Omar Khalid: external queue would add complexity, we prefer in-runtime bounded queues with smart rejection and graceful fallback. do you have a config for that?
[04:50] Lena Park: yes, I'll share a suggested config snippet today. It contains: concurrency_target=48, queue_max=500, fallback_policy=route_small_model, rejection_code=429, kv_cache_ttl=12h.
[05:05] Maya Chen: latency p99 was 1.2s earlier — any levers to bring that down other than queueing?
[05:12] Lena Park: quantization and kernel selection help; patch we applied swapped to int8 kernels for some operators and reduced per-token compute ~10%. also batching helps amortize per-request overhead. continuous batching was the biggest win.
[05:28] Priya Singh: side question: are we hitting memory limits on Dedicated nodes at high concurrency with 64?
[05:34] Diego Ramos: on Dedicated GPU pools, yes memory pressure increases. with 64 concurrency we see KV cache + batch state pushing close to GPU mem limits on the 48GB instance. we recommended 80-90% cap and prefer 80GB or multi-GPU sharding if you need sustained 64 concurrency.
[05:55] Omar Khalid: that would be an ops lift. we wanted Dedicated for predictability and data isolation though.
[06:02] Samir Patel: totally — Dedicated gives predictability but you pay for headroom. For a pilot I'd suggest running Hosted with reserved capacity to baseline costs and then move to Dedicated once you lock concurrency targets.
[06:16] Maya Chen: cost numbers? rough estimate for 48 target?
[06:19] Samir Patel: rough ballpark: Hosted reserved capacity to hit sustained 48 concurrency with your workload is about $Xk/month — I'll put exact numbers in the sheet.
[06:34] Ethan Brooks: please include per-token cost after batching and hit-rate assumptions.
[06:38] Samir Patel: will do.
[06:42] Maya Chen: back to tests — Omar will run a 24-hr stress with 64 ramp to see tail effects, right?
[06:48] Omar Khalid: yes, we'll run two test profiles: steady-state at 48 concurrency, and burst ramp to 64 for 30s every 10 minutes for 24 hours. collect traces and logs, and we'll share a single tarball.
[06:59] Lena Park: perfect. also include perf counters from the runtime so we can correlate KV cache hit-rate and batching stats. look for micro-batch sizes, queue wait times, and preemption events.
[07:12] Priya Singh: one more note — we saw occasional 500s in the early run. we think it was an orchestration flake during autoscale.
[07:20] Diego Ramos: yeah that was the early autoscaler misconfiguration — we've patched the bump algorithm, it should be smoother now. we'll mark the prior 500s as infra noise.
[07:28] Maya Chen: ok. any updates on security/compliance we've asked for? last week you promised SOC2 artifacts.
[07:34] Samir Patel: security pack is in the shared drive, redacted SOC2 attestation, SAML SSO guide, KMS integration notes. we'll re-share with the audit contact after this call.
[07:45] Ethan Brooks: great. can you also add a short write-up on audit log retention for private deployments?
[07:50] Samir Patel: will do. for Private (VPC) you get customer-controlled log retention and can ship to your SIEM.
[07:58] Maya Chen: timeline-wise, we want to decide by end of month about Dedicated procurement. is that still achievable?
[08:06] Samir Patel: yes, if the stress run looks good and latency tails are acceptable we can draft an order form early next week.
[08:12] Lena Park: quick note on metrics to watch during the 24h test: p95, p99, avg tokens/sec, micro-batch distribution, queue wait time histogram, KV cache hit-rate. please export histograms for tails.
[08:26] Omar Khalid: noted. we'll gather those.
[08:29] Maya Chen: on config changes, are any infra restarts required to change batching parameters?
[08:34] Diego Ramos: batching and concurrency params are dynamic — no node restarts required. kernel-level changes require rolling restart; the int8 kernel patch was already rolled in this morning.
[08:45] Priya Singh: good. what's the fallback model size you're recommending? 7B or 3B?
[08:50] Lena Park: for your scoring pipelines 3B worked fine, 7B is safer for open text. we recommend 3B for latency-sensitive non-critical paths.
[09:00] Maya Chen: can you add a sample routing policy? we want to see rules for tag-based routing to fallback.
[09:06] Lena Park: yes I'll include a policy sample: if request.tag == "critical" route to primary_model else route to queue->fallback when concurrency > cap.
[09:15] Ethan Brooks: any concerns about model drift when we occasionally route to smaller model?
[09:20] Lena Park: if you keep consistent evaluation sets and monitor quality, we can detect drift. Redwood Optimize can run periodic evals on sample traffic to surface regressions.
[09:30] Maya Chen: that'll be useful. ok last thing — can we get a summary email after the call with the key numbers and attached config?
[09:37] Samir Patel: yes, we'll send summary + config + updated bench sheet.
[09:41] Maya Chen: thanks.
[09:43] Samir Patel: great, appreciate everyone's time. quick recap: Lena to send config snippet, Omar runs 24h test, Samir uploads annotated benchmarks and pricing; follow-up demo scheduled next week.
[09:55] Maya Chen: thanks all. bye.
[10:00] [meeting end]
